summary: Defines the Connectivity Provisioning Negotiation Protocol (CPNP), a generic protocol for dynamically negotiating service parameters, for example for connectivity provisioning, storage facilities or content delivery networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you buy something, you and the seller go back and forth until you agree on terms. CPNP is a standard way for computers to haggle over the details of a network service.

subtitle: A protocol for automating negotiations over service parameters.

tldr.problem: Service providers need to negotiate terms with customers (bandwidth, pricing, features) but doing this manually is slow and error-prone. Each negotiation is unique and involves back-and-forth exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: CPNP defines a standard set of messages (quotation, offer, accept, decline) that a customer and provider use to negotiate service parameters, particularly for connectivity but applicable to any negotiated service.
tldr.outcome: Providers can automate customer order handling and service provisioning, reducing manual work and enabling dynamic agreement on service terms.

facts.value: 11 (QUOTATION, PROCESSING, OFFER, ACCEPT, DECLINE, ACK, CANCEL, WITHDRAW, UPDATE, FAIL, ACTIVATE)

facts.label: Maximum order identifiers
facts.value: Client-assigned (unique per client), server-assigned (unique per server)

today: RFC 8921 is an Informational RFC published in October 2020. It documents CPNP as a stable, extensible negotiation protocol applicable to any negotiable service, not just connectivity. The RFC is not on a standards track and specifies no IANA-managed registries, meaning CPNP implementations can extend it for their own purposes.

sections.title: What Is CPNP?
sections.content:
The Connectivity Provisioning Negotiation Protocol (CPNP) is a client-server protocol that automates the negotiation of service parameters between a customer and a provider. While designed primarily for negotiating connectivity services (like VPN bandwidth or quality of service), CPNP is generic and can negotiate any service parameters: cloud storage, content delivery networks, machine-to-machine services, or anything else with negotiable terms.

Instead of email and phone calls, both sides exchange structured messages. A customer sends what it needs, the provider responds with what it can offer, and they iterate until they reach an agreement (or both decide it is not going to work). The protocol is independent of the underlying transport and security: it can run over UDP with DTLS encryption, TCP with TLS, or other combinations.
sections.eli5: Imagine a vending machine that talks back. You say what snack you want and how much you will pay, the machine says if that deal works, and you either agree or make a counter-offer.

sections.title: The Quotation, Offer, Accept Pattern
sections.content:
CPNP uses a three-step negotiation model repeated as many times as needed. First, the customer sends a quotation order (a QUOTATION message) describing what service it needs and what terms it would accept. The quotation can specify exact values ("I need 100 Mbps") or loose ranges ("between 50 and 100 Mbps").

Second, the provider makes an offer (an OFFER message) describing what it can actually deliver. The offer reflects the provider's constraints: it might offer exactly what the customer asked for, or offer less ("I can only provide 80 Mbps"), or suggest alternatives ("10 Mbps is cheaper"). The provider includes an expiration time: the customer has until then to accept.

Third, the customer either accepts or declines (ACCEPT or DECLINE). If it accepts, both sides acknowledge and the agreement is final. If it declines, the customer can send a new quotation with different terms and start another round. This can repeat many times until they agree or both parties give up.

Once an agreement is reached, the customer can later update it (e.g., "add another VPN site") or withdraw it (cancel the service).
sections.eli5: Customer: "I want this." Provider: "I can offer you that." Customer: "Deal!" or "No, try again."

sections.title: The Messages
sections.content:
CPNP defines 11 message types, each carrying specific fields. A QUOTATION is the customer's request: it includes a unique order identifier (assigned by the customer), a transaction ID (for tracking), the service description, and optionally an expected response time ("I need an answer by Friday").

A PROCESSING message acknowledges receipt and signals the provider is working on it. The provider can use this to ask for more time ("I will have an offer by Tuesday") and the customer can accept (ACK) or reject (FAIL) the time extension.

An OFFER message is the provider's proposal. It includes a nonce (random number) and validity time so the customer cannot forge or replay old offers. The customer's ACCEPT copies the exact offer details back to prove it understood the terms.

A DECLINE message lets the customer reject an offer without accepting. The provider can send a FAIL message instead of offering anything, listing the reason: insufficient resources, authorization failed, or the request is outside the provider's domain.

Other messages handle post-agreement operations: UPDATE to modify the service (add or remove components), WITHDRAW to cancel, and ACTIVATE to turn a scheduled service on. An ACK confirms receipt of these messages.
sections.eli5: QUOTATION is "I want X"; OFFER is "you can have Y"; ACCEPT is "I agree to Y"; DECLINE is "no thanks"; FAIL is "I cannot help"; UPDATE is "change my order"; WITHDRAW is "cancel"; ACTIVATE is "turn it on".

sections.title: How Client and Server Behave
sections.content:
The client (customer) creates an order with an order identifier and sends a QUOTATION. It starts a timer: if no response arrives by the expected response time, it assumes the order was rejected. When the provider sends PROCESSING, the client notes the new timer (when the offer will arrive). If the timer expires without an offer, the order is cancelled.

When an OFFER arrives, the client has until the offer's validity time to decide. It can accept (send ACCEPT), decline (send DECLINE), or let the validity time expire (the offer is automatically retracted). The provider is unlikely to refuse an ACCEPT message since the provider made the offer, but the provider might refuse an UPDATE or ACTIVATE request if resources are not available.

The server (provider) receives a QUOTATION and assigns its own order identifier. It validates the request (does the customer have permission? are we the right provider?), checks internal policies (do we have resources?), and either makes an OFFER or sends FAIL. If it needs more time, it sends PROCESSING with a new expected offer time. The provider retains the order in its repository until the agreement is withdrawn or expires.

A key feature is parallel negotiations: a customer can send quotations to multiple providers simultaneously and pick the best offer. The CPNP client can also negotiate cascaded orders (child orders): if the provider needs resources from another provider, it acts as a client to negotiate with its upstream provider.
sections.eli5: Customer says "I want this by Friday." Provider says "I will have an offer by Wednesday." If the offer arrives by Wednesday, customer has until the validity time to decide. If not, the customer cancels.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
CPNP does not include built-in security; instead, it assumes an underlying security protocol such as DTLS (for UDP) or TLS (for TCP) encrypts and authenticates all messages. Both client and server must authenticate each other, and all data must be protected against eavesdropping and tampering.

CPNP protects against some attacks through message structure. Every quotation includes a transaction ID randomly generated by the client, making it hard to forge a reply from a spoofed server. Every offer includes a nonce (random number) assigned by the provider, preventing a malicious third party from accepting an old offer on behalf of someone else. The protocol uses sequence numbers that must increase in every message, blocking replay attacks (resending an old message to undo an action).

Providers must enforce access control (only authorized customers can place orders) and implement rate limiting to defend against denial-of-service attacks (an attacker sending thousands of QUOTATION messages). Customer information (contact details, the types of services requested) is privacy-sensitive and must not be shared with third parties without consent.
sections.eli5: Think of it like a sealed, signed letter. Encryption hides the content, a signature proves who sent it, and a unique ID on every letter prevents someone from forging a reply or sending an old letter again.

sections.title: How CPNP Fits into Networks
sections.content:
CPNP is one piece of a larger system. A provider's CPNP server is connected to internal modules that help it make decisions: a network topology database (what routes and capacity are available), a resource manager (are we overbooked?), a customer profile database (is this customer authorized? what prices apply?), and business rules (what kinds of orders do we automatically approve?).

Once an agreement is final, CPNP is done; the provider hands the order off to other systems. For a connectivity order, the provider might use NETCONF (a network configuration protocol) or RESTCONF (a REST API) to configure the actual routers and links to activate the service. CPNP and its successors handle negotiation and service activation; other protocols handle the details of configuring the network itself.

Use cases include Layer 3 VPN negotiation (enterprise customers ordering site-to-site connectivity), inter-domain services (two telecom networks negotiating interconnection), CDN expansion (content delivery networks sharing infrastructure), cloud resource provisioning (customers requesting compute and storage), and network slicing (requesting custom network partitions with specific guarantees).
sections.eli5: CPNP is the front desk of a service provider: it handles the negotiation. Behind it are databases and business logic that actually make it happen. After a deal is done, other tools activate the actual service.
